title: Nālāyira Divya Prabandham
summary: The 'four thousand divine compositions': the collected hymns of the twelve Āḻvārs (with Tiruvaraṅkattu Amutaṉār's Irāmāṉuca Nūṟṟantāti), gathered and arranged by Nāthamuni, set to music for temple recitation, and revered by Śrīvaiṣṇavas as the Tamil Veda. It sings Tirumāl with Śrī in his temple images, the avatāras, surrender, service, the name, and love in the voices of Tamil love-poetry.

attribution.tradition: Sung by the twelve Āḻvārs; lost and recovered by Nāthamuni, who received all four thousand from Nammāḻvār in yogic vision at Kurukūr after reciting Madhurakavi's Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu 12,000 times.
attribution.scholarly: Compiled c. 10th c. CE from hymns composed c. 6th–9th c.; the four-part arrangement and the inclusion of the Irāmāṉuca Nūṟṟantāti reflect later Śrīvaiṣṇava redaction.

tradition.text: hymns of the late Dvāpara and early Kali ages, recovered by Nāthamuni

scholarly.text: hymns c. 6th–9th c. CE; compiled c. 10th c. CE

structure.description: About 4000 verses in four 'thousands' (āyiram): (1) Mutalāyiram (c. 947: Tiruppallāṇṭu, Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi, Tiruppāvai, Nācciyār Tirumoḻi, Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi, Tiruccanta Viruttam, Tirumālai, Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci, Amalaṉātipirāṉ, Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu); (2) Periya Tirumoḻi with Tirukkuṟuntāṇṭakam and Tiruneṭuntāṇṭakam (c. 1134); (3) Iyaṟpā, the recited portion (c. 817: the first three Tiruvantātis, Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti, Tiruviruttam, Tiruvāciriyam, Periya Tiruvantāti, Tiruveḻukkūṟṟirukkai, Ciṟiya and Periya Tirumaṭal, Irāmāṉuca Nūṟṟantāti); (4) Tiruvāymoḻi (1102). Each work is preceded by invocatory taṉiyaṉ verses.

notes: Part counts (947 / 1134 / 817 / 1102 = 4000) as recalled, counting Ciṟiya Tirumaṭal as 40 and Periya Tirumaṭal as 78 units; placement of Tirukkuṟuntāṇṭakam/Tiruneṭuntāṇṭakam differs in some arrangements. Commentaries: see src:tiruvaymoli and the U14 commentary entries (src:arayirappati etc.). Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai commented on nearly the whole Prabandham.

title: Tiruvāymoḻi
summary: Nammāḻvār's hundred decads (1102 verses), the fourth thousand of the Prabandham and the 'Tamil Upaniṣad' (Draviḍopaniṣad) of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas: the Lord's supremacy and accessibility, the gift of knowledge-and-love, surrender at Tiruvēṅkaṭam, service, love-longing in the voice of the girl Parāṅkuśa-nāyakī, her mother and friend, and in the last decads the soul's journey on the path of light and final union.

structure.description: 1102 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: born in the first year of the Kali age (hagiographies; one account gives the 43rd day)

attribution.tradition: Sung by Nammāḻvār at Kurukūr; held to be the Sāmaveda in Tamil.

notes: Structure: 10 centums (pattu) × 10 decads (tiruvāymoḻi), mostly 11 verses each (10 + a phalaśruti). Commentaries (U14 entries): Ārāyirappaṭi (Tirukkurukaippirāṉ Piḷḷāṉ), Oṉpatiṉāyirappaṭi (Nañjīyar), Irupattunālāyirappaṭi (Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai), Īṭu Muppattāṟāyirappaṭi (Vaṭakku Tiruvīti Piḷḷai, from Nampiḷḷai's lectures), Paṉṉīrāyirappaṭi (Vādikesari Aḻagiya Maṇavāḷa Jīyar); Sanskrit: Deśika's Dramiḍopaniṣat-tātparya-ratnāvalī and Dramiḍopaniṣat-sāra; Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's Tiruvāymoḻi Nūṟṟantāti. Tiruvāymoḻi refs are centum.decad.verse (patt.tiruvāymoḻi.pācuram).

title: Tiruviruttam
summary: Nammāḻvār's hundred verses in the viruttam metre, a love-poem sequence in the akam mode; opens with the prayer to be freed from false knowledge, evil conduct and the impure body. Held to be the Ṛgveda in Tamil.

structure.description: 100 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: born in the first year of the Kali age (hagiographies; one account gives the 43rd day)

title: Tiruvāciriyam
summary: Nammāḻvār's seven long verses in the āciriyam metre on the Lord's cosmic form and glory. Held to be the Yajurveda in Tamil.

structure.description: 7 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: born in the first year of the Kali age (hagiographies; one account gives the 43rd day)

title: Periya Tiruvantāti
summary: Nammāḻvār's 87 veṇpā verses in antāti chain, in which the Āḻvār speaks with his own heart about the Lord's greatness and nearness. Held to be the Atharvaveda in Tamil.

structure.description: 87 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: born in the first year of the Kali age (hagiographies; one account gives the 43rd day)

title: Mutal Tiruvantāti
summary: Poykai Āḻvār's hundred veṇpās, the 'first' antāti, sung (in the tradition's account) in the dark vestibule at Tirukkōvalūr: it opens by lighting a lamp with the earth as bowl, the sea as ghee and the sun as flame.

structure.description: 100 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Iraṇṭām Tiruvantāti
summary: Pūtattāḻvār's hundred veṇpās, the 'second' antāti, opening with the lamp of love lit for Nāraṇaṉ.

structure.description: 100 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Mūṉṟām Tiruvantāti
summary: Pēyāḻvār's hundred veṇpās, the 'third' antāti, opening with the vision in the lamplight: 'I have seen Śrī, I have seen the golden form ...'.

structure.description: 100 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti
summary: Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār's 96 veṇpās, opening 'Nārāyaṇa created the four-faced one' — a sustained assertion of Nārāyaṇa's supremacy over Brahmā and Śiva and of refuge in him alone.

structure.description: 96 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Tiruccanta Viruttam
summary: Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār's 120 verses in the canta-viruttam metre on the Lord as cause of all, his avatāras and his reclining image at Kuṭantai (Kumbakōṇam) and other sites.

structure.description: 120 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu
summary: Madhurakavi Āḻvār's eleven verses addressed not to Viṣṇu but to his teacher Nammāḻvār: saying 'the Nampi of southern Kurukūr' is sweeter than approaching Kṛṣṇa himself; 'I know no other god'. The model of devotion to the teacher; the text Nāthamuni recited to recover the Prabandham.

structure.description: 11 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

tradition.text: born in the first year of the Kali age (hagiographies; one account gives the 43rd day)

title: Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi
summary: Kulaśekhara Āḻvār's 105 verses in ten decads: longing to live among devotees at Śrīraṅgam, to be born even as a fish or a step at Tiruvēṅkaṭam, clinging to the Lord of Vittuvakkōṭu though he cause grief, Devakī's and Daśaratha's laments, and a lullaby for Rāma.

structure.description: 105 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Mukundamālā
summary: Sanskrit hymn to Mukunda (Kṛṣṇa) attributed to Kulaśekhara: the devotee asks not for dharma, wealth or pleasure but only for unwavering devotion to the Lord's feet in every birth, and asks that the mind enter the Lord's feet now, since at death, with the throat choked, remembrance may fail.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Kulaśekhara Āḻvār, the king-devotee of Kerala.
attribution.scholarly: Commonly accepted as by a Kulaśekhara of Kerala; the identification with the Āḻvār and with the author of the Sanskrit dramas Tapatīsaṃvaraṇa and Subhadrādhanañjaya is debated.

scholarly.text: c. 9th c. CE if by the Āḻvār

structure.description: c. 34–40 verses; recensions differ in number and order

notes: Verse numbers differ between recensions; teachings are therefore cited by incipit.

title: Tiruppallāṇṭu (of Periyāḻvār)
summary: Periyāḻvār's twelve-verse benediction 'many years, many years' for the Lord's safety — the devotee, fearing the evil eye on the Lord who appeared on Garuḍa, prays for his welfare (maṅgaḷāśāsana) and invites servants of the Lord to join; it opens the Prabandham and daily worship.

structure.description: 12 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

notes: Distinct from the Śaiva Tiruppallāṇṭu of Cēntaṉār (src:tiruppallantu, U18).

title: Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi
summary: Periyāḻvār's 461 verses: Kṛṣṇa's birth and childhood sung through Yaśodā's eyes (the first Tamil piḷḷaittamiḻ of the child-god), the Lord at the temples, and the Āḻvār's own surrender, including his plea made in advance for the hour of death.

structure.description: 461 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Tiruppāvai
summary: Āṇṭāḷ's thirty verses of the Mārkaḻi vow (pāvai nōṉpu): the cowherd girls of Āyarpāṭi rise before dawn, wake one another, go to Nandagopa's house, wake Nappiṉṉai and Kṛṣṇa, and ask for the 'drum' (paṟai) — which in the end is revealed as unbroken kinship with him and service to him alone through seven times seven births.

structure.description: 30 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

notes: Scholarly dating uses verse 13 ('Venus has risen, Jupiter has set') for astronomical estimates (8th–9th c.); tradition places Āṇṭāḷ in the early Kali age. Sung throughout South India in the month of Mārkaḻi.

title: Nācciyār Tirumoḻi
summary: Āṇṭāḷ's 143 verses in 14 decads: prayer to Kāma to unite her with Kṛṣṇa, the dream of her wedding ('vāraṇam āyiram'), questions to the conch about the taste of his lips, messages to clouds and birds, the agony of separation, and at the end the sight of him in Vṛndāvana.

structure.description: 143 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Tirumālai
summary: Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Āḻvār's 45 verses (the 'sacred garland') to the Lord of Śrīraṅgam: the sweetness of his names above Indra's kingdom, the Āḻvār's confession that he has no virtue, and the teaching that devotees of any birth are to be honoured while reviling them makes even Veda-learned brāhmaṇas outcaste.

structure.description: 45 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci (of Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Āḻvār)
summary: Ten verses awakening the Lord of Śrīraṅgam at dawn, the gods and sages waiting at his door; the Āḻvār asks to be made servant to the Lord's servants. Sung daily at dawn in Śrīvaiṣṇava temples.

structure.description: 10 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

notes: Distinct from Māṇikkavācakar's Śaiva Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci in the Tiruvācakam.

title: Amalaṉātipirāṉ
summary: Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār's ten verses sung when carried into the Śrīraṅgam sanctum: the Lord's form described from his feet to his face, ending 'the eyes that have seen my nectar will see nothing else'.

structure.description: 10 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

title: Periya Tirumoḻi
summary: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār's 1084 verses in eleven centums: the discovery of the name 'Nārāyaṇa' after a life of wrongdoing, pilgrimage hymns to some eighty sites, the Lord's avatāras, and love-longing as Parakāla-nāyakī.

structure.description: 1084 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, r. c. 731–796)

title: Tirukkuṟuntāṇṭakam
summary: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār's twenty short tāṇṭakam verses on the Lord who entered his heart and on the name.

structure.description: 20 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, r. c. 731–796)

title: Tiruneṭuntāṇṭakam
summary: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār's thirty long tāṇṭakam verses: first in his own voice, then in the voice of the mother describing her love-sick daughter, then in the voice of the girl (Parakāla-nāyakī) herself. By tradition the text through which Parāśara Bhaṭṭar won over the Advaitin who became Nañjīyar, hence recited at the opening of the recitation festival.

structure.description: 30 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, r. c. 731–796)

notes: The three-voice division (1–10 own voice, 11–20 mother, 21–30 heroine) is as recalled; check.

title: Tiruveḻukkūṟṟirukkai
summary: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār's single poem built as a chariot (ratha-bandha): its lines climb and descend through the numbers one to seven, each number woven into a deed or attribute of the Lord at Kuṭantai.

structure.description: 1 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, r. c. 731–796)

title: Ciṟiya Tirumaṭal
summary: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār's shorter maṭal poem: Parakāla-nāyakī, spurned by the Lord, threatens to 'ride the maṭal' (the palmyra-stem horse) through the streets to shame him — a threat that Tamil convention allowed only to men.

structure.description: 40 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, r. c. 731–796)

title: Periya Tirumaṭal
summary: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār's longer maṭal poem on the same theme, cataloguing the Lord's deeds and sites as the heroine's grounds of complaint.

structure.description: 78 verses (pācurams) as counted in the Prabandham

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla, r. c. 731–796)

title: Paripāṭal
summary: One of the eight Saṅgam anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai): hymns in the paripāṭal metre, of which about two dozen survive, several to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu), others to Cevvēḷ (Murukaṉ) and the river Vaiyai; its Tirumāl hymns praise him as the source and substance of all things and name his hill-shrine Tirumāliruñcōlai. A precursor of Āḻvār devotion, not an Āḻvār text.
notes: Placed with lin:alvar as the earliest Tamil devotional hymns to Tirumāl; it belongs to Saṅgam literature, for which no lineage entry exists. Many poets; attributions per hymn are given in the colophons and not recorded here.

title: Irāmāvatāram (Kamba Rāmāyaṇam)
summary: Kampaṉ's Tamil Rāmāyaṇa in six kāṇṭams, a devotional retelling of Rāma's story that opens by taking refuge in the Lord who creates, sustains and dissolves the worlds in play; by tradition first recited (araṅkēṟṟam) before Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Kampaṉ of Tiruvaḻuntūr under the patron Caṭaiyappa Vaḷḷal; approved at Śrīraṅgam.
attribution.scholarly: Kampaṉ, c. 12th c. CE (some scholars 9th c.); the Uttara Kāṇṭam is ascribed to Oṭṭakkūttar.

structure.description: six kāṇṭams (Pāla to Yuddha), c. 10,000+ verses; Uttara Kāṇṭam a later addition

notes: Kampaṉ is not an Āḻvār; placed with lin:alvar as Tamil Vaiṣṇava devotional literature of the Āḻvār milieu (tradition links him to Nammāḻvār through the Caṭakōpar Antāti). U05 covers Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa.

title: Caṭakōpar Antāti
summary: A hundred-verse antāti in praise of Nammāḻvār (Caṭakōpaṉ) attributed to Kampaṉ.

scholarly.text: c. 12th c. CE if by Kampaṉ

notes: Attribution to Kampaṉ is the tradition's; tradition says he composed it so that his Rāmāyaṇa would be accepted at Śrīraṅgam. Verse count as recalled.

title: Prabandhasāram
summary: Vedānta Deśika's Tamil verse summary of the Āḻvārs: their birthplaces, birth-stars and months, and the names and verse-counts of their works.
notes: Existence recalled with moderate confidence; contents summarised from memory.

title: Munivāhanabhoga
summary: Vedānta Deśika's commentary on Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār's Amalaṉātipirāṉ (the Āḻvār 'carried by the sage', munivāhana), reading its ten verses as containing the essence of Vedānta.

title: Nārada Bhakti Sūtra
summary: Eighty-four aphorisms attributed to the sage Nārada defining devotion as supreme love (parama-prema) of the nature of nectar, 'the fruit itself', higher than action, knowledge and yoga; they give earlier teachers' definitions and the gopīs as the model, the means (renunciation, unceasing worship, hearing and singing, above all the grace of great souls), the things to avoid, the signs of the lover of God, the eleven forms of attachment, and the line of bhakti teachers.

attribution.tradition: Spoken by the divine sage Nārada ('nārada-proktam', NBS 84).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; usually dated after the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, c. 10th–13th c. CE or later.

scholarly.text: c. 10th–13th c. CE or later (no consensus)

structure.description: 84 sūtras (numbering varies slightly between editions); sometimes divided into five chapters (adhyāyas) in modern editions

notes: Sūtra numbering follows the common 84-sūtra text; some editions divide or join sūtras differently, so numbers may shift by one or two. No pre-modern Sanskrit commentary recalled with confidence; modern commentaries are many (e.g. in the Ramakrishna and ISKCON movements) and are not recorded here.

title: Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra
summary: One hundred aphorisms attributed to the sage Śāṇḍilya, opening 'Now, therefore, the inquiry into devotion' and defining devotion as supreme attachment (parānurakti) to the Lord; it argues that devotion is not knowledge or an act, that it is primary and the others subordinate, distinguishes secondary (gauṇī) devotion leading to the supreme, reports Kāśyapa's and Bādarāyaṇa's views on devotion's object, and discusses eligibility, the Lord, the soul and creation.

attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; perhaps earlier than the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra; usually placed c. 10th–12th c. CE (no consensus).

structure.description: 100 sūtras in three adhyāyas, each of two āhnikas

notes: Continuous sūtra numbering (100 sūtras in 3 adhyāyas × 2 āhnikas) as recalled; exact numbers not checked — verify against Svapneśvara's edition.

title: Śāṇḍilyabhaktisūtrabhāṣya (of Svapneśvara)
summary: Svapneśvara's commentary, the standard exposition of the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra, reading devotion within a Vedāntic frame.
notes: Svapneśvara's date and region are uncertain; the commentary's doctrinal leaning is recalled only in general terms.

title: Bhakticandrikā
summary: A commentary on the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra ascribed to Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha.
notes: Recalled as printed with the sūtras (Sarasvatī Bhavana series); which Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha wrote it is uncertain — several authors share the name (see tch:narayana-tirtha).

title: Muktāphala
summary: Vopadeva's anthology of Bhāgavata verses arranged under the themes of devotion (the Lord, his avatāras, the forms and fruits of devotion, and the devotional rasas), with the commentary Kaivalyadīpikā by Hemādri.
notes: The arrangement by nine devotional rasas is recalled with low confidence.

title: Kaivalyadīpikā
summary: Hemādri's commentary on Vopadeva's Muktāphala.

title: Bhaktiratnāvalī
summary: Viṣṇupurī's anthology of Bhāgavata verses on devotion, arranged by the forms of devotion, with his own commentary Kāntimālā.
notes: Author's region (Tirhut/Mithilā) and date recalled with low confidence; arrangement 'by the nine forms' recalled with low confidence.

title: Gīta Govinda
summary: Jayadeva's Sanskrit song-poem in twelve cantos and twenty-four songs (aṣṭapadīs, each set to a named rāga and tāla) with linking verses: Kṛṣṇa's spring dance with the cowherd women, Rādhā's jealousy and withdrawal, the longing of both in separation carried by Rādhā's friend, Kṛṣṇa's plea for forgiveness, and their union. It opens with a hymn to the ten avatāras borne by Kṛṣṇa and offers itself to those whose minds delight in remembering Hari and in the arts of love.

attribution.tradition: Composed by Jayadeva, son of Bhojadeva and Rāmādevī (as the closing verse says), in the service of Jagannātha at Purī (Odisha account) or at the Bengal court of Lakṣmaṇasena (Bengal account); by tradition Kṛṣṇa himself wrote one line (10th canto).
attribution.scholarly: Jayadeva, 12th c. CE; the opening names poets of Lakṣmaṇasena's court (Umāpatidhara, Śaraṇa, Govardhana, Dhoyī); his birthplace (Kenduli in Bengal or Kenduli Sasan in Odisha, or Mithilā) is disputed.

structure.description: 12 sargas (cantos) with 24 aṣṭapadī songs and interspersed ślokas; canto titles as commonly printed: Sāmoda-dāmodara, Akleśa-keśava, Mugdha-madhusūdana, Snigdha-madhusūdana, Sākāṅkṣa-puṇḍarīkākṣa, Dhṛṣṭa-vaikuṇṭha, Nāgara-nārāyaṇa, Vilakṣa-lakṣmīpati, Mugdha-mukunda, Catura-caturbhuja, Sānanda-dāmodara, Suprīta-pītāmbara (variants exist)

notes: Liturgical use: sung daily before Jagannātha at Purī (by tradition confirmed by an order of Gajapati Pratāparudra, c. 1499, that the temple singers sing only the Gīta Govinda — recalled with moderate confidence); sung in Kerala temples as aṣṭapadī (sopāna saṅgītam) and in South Indian bhajana; relished by Caitanya (Caitanya Caritāmṛta); two of Jayadeva's hymns (not from the Gīta Govinda) are in the Sikh Ādi Granth (context only). Canto-title list: moderate/low confidence. Not to be confused with the later Jayadeva (Pīyūṣavarṣa) of the Candrāloka and Prasannarāghava.

title: Rasikapriyā
summary: Mahārāṇā Kumbhakarṇa (Kumbhā) of Mewar's commentary on the Gīta Govinda, explaining its poetics, rāgas and meaning.

title: Kṛṣṇagīti
summary: Mānaveda's Sanskrit song-drama on Kṛṣṇa's life, modelled on the Gīta Govinda, which became the text of the Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam dance-drama of Guruvāyūr in Kerala.
notes: Lineage placement: Kerala temple performance tradition (lin:kerala-tantra, U08) as nearest available lineage.
